title: Trade error write-up: duplicate child orders on 6/30 close
text:
Hi Daniel,

Following up on yesterday's issue, here is the write-up. During the closing auction on 6/30, a parent order in OMS was amended while two child slices were still working at the venue. The amend did not cancel the working slices, so the algo re-sent the residual and we ended up with roughly 18,400 shares of duplicate fills, about $412K notional. We caught it at 4:07 PM when the TradeBlotter position did not match the desk's expected position.

Impact: we closed out the excess in the auction at a net loss of about $3,150 versus arrival. No client was disadvantaged; the error was absorbed in the firm error account.

Root cause: the amend workflow in OMS lets a trader edit quantity without a hard check on live child orders. I should have cancelled the slices first, and that is on me.

Next steps: I will file a ticket with Technology for a pre-amend validation, and I will add a checklist step to the desk's close procedures. Happy to walk through the timeline with Marcus and Ravi if useful.

Thanks,
Travis

title: Supervisory guidance: digital-asset client onboarding and custody
text:
Dear Mr. Bell,

The examination team of the Office of Financial Supervision writes to draw your attention to interim guidance recently issued by this Office on the onboarding and servicing of clients whose wealth derives, in whole or in material part, from digital assets.

The interim guidance sets out the Office's expectations for regulated institutions in three areas.

First, anti-money laundering controls. Transaction monitoring should be able to trace relevant on-chain flows, including the provenance of assets before conversion to fiat. Institutions should be able to identify exposure to mixers, sanctioned addresses and high-risk exchanges.

Second, custody due diligence. Where client assets are held with, or flow through, third-party digital-asset custodians, the institution should document its due diligence on those custodians. This includes their control environment, segregation of client assets and regulatory standing.

Third, source-of-funds and source-of-wealth verification. Verification should be supported by evidence that an examiner can independently review, not by client attestation alone.

Given Halcyon Ridge Capital's wealth management and lending activities, we ask that the firm submit a written risk assessment by August 29, 2026. The assessment should address:
- the firm's current and prospective exposure to digital-asset-derived clients;
- the adequacy of existing AML, KYC and sanctions screening controls against the expectations above;
- any remediation planned, with timelines.

Final guidance is expected later this year. The Office may take your response into account in scoping the firm's next examination.

Please direct questions to the examination team at this address.

Sincerely,

Examination Division
Office of Financial Supervision

title: FRAUD-2291 preliminary review
text:
Hi Marcus,

Here is my preliminary write-up on FRAUD-2291 (FraudScore transaction t_r016), following your note in #compliance on Friday. It covers the money trail only. The connection analysis is still outstanding (see Next steps).

Summary
The pattern looks like layering through a newly opened wealth account. There are four phases.

1. August: structured funding. Through August the account received a string of ACH credits, each kept under $10,000. None of them tripped a CTR-style threshold on its own, but the cadence and the near-identical amounts look deliberate. Taken together they don't match the funding profile captured at onboarding.

2. Sep 25: the inbound wire. At 10:14 ET a $48,000.00 inbound wire arrived from Coastal Meridian Trading Ltd (Cyprus). That is the transaction FraudScore flagged. I found nothing tying the originator to the client's stated source of wealth or occupation.

3. Sep 25-28: internal transfers. Within hours the funds started moving to several other Halcyon accounts in internal book transfers. Every one was under $10,000, mostly in the $9,200-$9,900 range. Almost all of the $48k had left the original account within about three business days.

4. Sep 29-30: outbound wires to crypto. On Sep 29 and Sep 30 the receiving accounts sent outgoing wires through PaymentsGateway to Bitrail Digital Exchange, a US crypto exchange, beneficiary account ⟨ACCT_0629⟩. Several separate Halcyon accounts all wiring to the same exchange beneficiary within a two-day window is the part that concerns me most.

What I have not done yet
I have not checked whether the receiving accounts share phone numbers, home addresses, or login devices. That is my next step. I plan to pull the ClientHub contact records and the online banking session and device data for each account. If they overlap, we are probably looking at a coordinated ring rather than one bad actor.

Assessment
The sequence fits a classic placement-layering pattern: structured deposits, a large offshore wire, fragmentation under $10k, then exit to crypto. I think a SAR is likely here, but I want the connection analysis done before we commit to a narrative.

Ask
Can I have your approval to formally escalate this? That would mean opening a case in AMLMonitor and pulling in the RMs on the affected accounts on a need-to-know basis. Jenna, I've copied you because I'll need help extracting the session and device data for the linkage work. I also want to confirm that the FraudScore rules would catch a repeat of this pattern.

Thanks,
Nadia
